paragraphs.heading: A cover that breathes with the seasons
paragraphs.text: The Arctic ice pack is the sea ice that covers the Arctic Ocean and the waters near it. It follows a regular yearly cycle: ice melts through spring and summer, shrinks to its smallest around mid-September, and then grows again through autumn and winter. In summer the cover is about half of what it is in winter. Some ice lasts from one year to the next. This multi-year ice now makes up 28% of the sea ice in the Arctic basin, and it is thicker than seasonal ice, up to 3–4 m thick across large areas, and its ridges are up to 20 m thick.

paragraphs.heading: A lid and a mirror
paragraphs.text: Sea ice matters a great deal for the heat balance of the polar oceans. It acts as insulation between the ocean, which is relatively warm, and the much colder air over it, so the ocean loses less heat. It is also very reflective. Bare ice sends back about 60% of the solar radiation that reaches it, and snow-covered ice about 80%. That is much more than the sea, which reflects about 10%, so the ice also affects how much sunlight is absorbed at the surface.

paragraphs.heading: Salt left behind
paragraphs.text: The freezing cycle is also an important source of dense, salty water. When sea water freezes, most of its salt stays behind in the water. The surface water that remains is made dense by the extra salt, so it sinks. This is how dense water masses like North Atlantic Deep Water are produced. This production of dense water is essential in maintaining a circulation known as the thermohaline circulation, and representing it accurately is important in climate modelling.

paragraphs.heading: How the ice is measured
paragraphs.text: The Hadley Centre in the United Kingdom holds Arctic sea ice records that reach back to the turn of the 20th century, though the quality of the data before 1950 is debatable. Reliable measurements of the ice edge begin within the satellite era. From the late 1970s, a microwave instrument on the Seasat and Nimbus 7 satellites gave information that did not depend on sunlight or weather conditions. Two quantities are estimated, area and extent. Extent counts any area of ocean that has at least 15% sea ice, and it is the larger of the two.

paragraphs.heading: The long decline
paragraphs.text: Besides the seasonal cycle, Arctic sea ice has shown an underlying declining trend in recent decades. From 1979 to 2002 ice extent fell by 2.5% ± 0.9% per decade, a statistically significant decrease. The trend in the September minimum extent for 1979–2011 was a decline of 12.0% per decade. In 2007 the minimum extent dropped by over a million square kilometers, to 4,140,000 km², the largest decline since accurate satellite data became available. A new record low followed in 2012, at about 3,500,000 km².

paragraphs.heading: Thickness counts too
paragraphs.text: The volume of sea ice depends on how thick the ice is as well as on the area it covers. One computer-based calculation of ice volume found that monitoring volume is much more significant for judging sea ice loss than area alone. A modeling study of 1947 to 1999 found a statistically significant trend in ice volume of −3% per decade, and when the trend was split into a wind-forced part and a temperature-forced part, essentially all of it came from temperature. Satellites have made it easier to measure trends in extent, but measuring thickness accurately remains a challenge. As more and more of the ice is thinner first-year ice, storms have a greater effect on its stability, and turbulence from major extratropical cyclones results in extensive fractures.
